newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Albright takes tough talks from Croatia to Serbia.
newsitem.headline: Albright takes tough talks from Croatia to Serbia.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright took her tough approach to Balkan peace to Serbia on Saturday but seemed to have treated Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic more lightly than his Croatian counterpart.

In a show of undiplomatic bluntness, Albright publicly scolded Croatian President Franjo Tudjman in the morning for his failure to comply with commitments made in the Dayton peace accord which ended the Bosnian war in 1995.
But at her second stop on her first whistle-stop tour of the region, Albright seemed to have softened her language.

She held talks with Milosevic immediately after arriving in Belgrade and did not elaborate afterwards on their content, though discussions were expected to cover issues including war crimes, the return of refugees and problems with political and media freedoms in Serbia.
"The talks were very frank and useful," she told reporters. "I laid down what has to be done in order to develop better relations between our countries."
Milosevic said the talks were very open and "in the spirit of tradition between our two countries in their long history".
"I am certain that we will achieve better and better progress as regards the questions we discussed, and normalise our relations step by step."

There was no mention of statements made recently in Washington that the United States would continue to deprive Belgrade of international aid and diplomatic recognition if it did not meet certain demands, including compliance with the Dayton accords.
After talking with other representatives of both delegations, Albright held one-to-one talks with Milosevic.
Her spokesman told reporters that Albright was "very displeased with the record of the Serbian government on the Dayton peace accord".
He added that he did not expect to see normalisation of relations between the two countries soon.
"I don't think that is possible until the issue of war crimes, the issue of democracy, or the lack of it, in Serbia is taken care of. Until then I don't expect a normal relationship.

"We don't have an ambassador here, we don't recognise Yugoslavia's seat in the United Nations...I am sorry to say that because this is not good for the Serbian people here but the government is not cooperating."
After meeting Milosevic, Albright walked to the Czech embassy near the Serbian presidency buildings to the amazement of onlookers who never see high officials walking the streets.
She lived in the embassy as a child when her father was a diplomat in Belgrade.

Albright had earlier threatened in Zagreb that the United States would consider blocking International Monetary Fund loans to Zagreb and stall Croatia's integration into Western institutions if it did not comply with the Dayton accords.
A U.S. official said later Albright told Tudjman she would personally approve how the United States voted at the IMF.

Officials described Albright's meeting with Tudjman as the toughest she has had with any leader since becoming secretary of state in January. She told him it was morally unacceptable to have an ethnically pure state in modern Europe, and is likely to have sent a similar message to Milosevic.

Albright's plain speaking on her first tour of the Balkans as Secretary of State signals a tougher approach from the United States, which is determined to see the fulfilment of the Dayton agreement -- particularly in areas concerning war criminals and the return of refugees.

Both Milosevic and Tudjman signed the document which allows for all refugees to return home, though Zagreb has been heavily criticised after some Croatian Serbs were attacked when they returned to their pre-war homes in Croatia.

Albright asked Tudjman to use his influence in the Bosnian-Croat areas of Bosnia to turn over indicted war criminals thought to be hiding there. Milosevic is also under pressure from the Americans to hand over indicted Serbs.
